passage:
In Class 5, Farida was my best friend. We sat together, shared tiffin, walked home together every day.

Then a new girl, Rhea, joined. Farida started sitting with her at lunch. They laughed at jokes I didn't get.

I felt sick every lunchtime. I kept thinking Farida would forget me. I even said something mean about Rhea's bag, which I'm not proud of.

One day Farida asked, "Why are you so grumpy?" I told her the truth: "I'm scared you like her more."

She laughed and hugged me. "I can have two friends, silly."

I'm Charu, and the three of us ate together after that.

qa.q: What did Charu say about Rhea's bag?
qa.a: Charu said something mean about Rhea's bag.

qa.q: What was Charu afraid of when Farida sat with Rhea?
qa.a: Charu felt jealous and scared, afraid of losing Farida to the new girl.

qa.q: What helped Charu handle the jealousy?
qa.a: Telling Farida the truth about the fear, instead of staying grumpy, let them talk it through.

qa.q: How might Rhea have felt when Charu was mean about her bag?
qa.a: Rhea may have felt hurt or confused, not knowing why Charu disliked her.

grounding: A child looks back on feeling jealous when a best friend grew close to a new girl, and talking about the fear.

passage:
Teacher's note, Christmas term.

Sarita and Meenu have been best friends all year. For the Christmas carol duet, Meenu chose Tina as her partner instead of Sarita.

Sarita went very quiet. At break she snapped at Tina and told Meenu, "Fine, go sing with her." Later she cried in the corridor. She said, "Meenu will like Tina more now."

I sat with her and said it's normal to feel scared of losing a friend. I suggested she tell Meenu how she felt. She did at lunch. Meenu said the duet was only because Tina's voice matched hers.

— Hansa

qa.q: Who did Meenu choose for the duet?
qa.a: Meenu chose Tina as her partner.

qa.q: What was Sarita feeling when she snapped at Tina?
qa.a: Sarita was jealous and afraid of losing Meenu's friendship to Tina.

qa.q: How did Hansa help Sarita with her jealousy?
qa.a: Hansa sat with her, said the fear was normal, and suggested talking honestly to Meenu.

qa.q: How might Tina have felt when Sarita snapped at her?
qa.a: Tina may have felt hurt or confused, since she only sang with Meenu for the duet.

grounding: A teacher notes a child's jealousy when her best friend picks another partner, and helps her talk about it.

passage:
Onam, Sunday

Aadhya came from Dubai for Onam, and suddenly Ammachi only talks to her. Aadhya helped make the pookalam. Aadhya sang the song. Aadhya got the first payasam.

I've been Ammachi's favourite since forever. She always calls me her "kutti". Today she didn't call me that even once.

I went and sat on the back steps and didn't come for the sadya until Amma called twice.

Then Ammachi came out and sat next to me. "Thomas, Aadhya is here for ten days. You're here every day." She gave me a whole banana chip packet.

I still feel a bit weird. But less.

qa.q: Where did Aadhya come from?
qa.a: Aadhya came from Dubai for Onam.

qa.q: How did Thomas feel when Ammachi paid attention to Aadhya?
qa.a: Thomas felt jealous and hurt, afraid of losing the place as Ammachi's favourite.

qa.q: How did Ammachi help Thomas?
qa.a: She came and sat with Thomas and reassured that their bond stays, since Thomas is there every day.

qa.q: How might Aadhya feel if she knew Thomas was upset?
qa.a: Aadhya might feel surprised or sorry, since she was only enjoying her short visit.

grounding: During Onam, a child feels jealous when a visiting cousin gets the grandmother's attention, and is reassured.

passage:
Tuesday

Leela got a new cycle with GEARS. Seven gears. It's blue and shiny and she rode it round the colony three times while everyone watched.

My cycle is Didi's old one. The bell doesn't ring and the seat is too low.

I wanted to say "nice cycle" but it came out as "it's too big for you." Which isn't true.

I keep imagining riding it. I want everyone to watch me like that.

Maybe I'll ask Papa if we can fix my bell and raise my seat. And tomorrow I'll tell Leela it really is nice.

Hansa

qa.q: How many gears does Leela's cycle have?
qa.a: Seven gears.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling watching Leela ride the new cycle?
qa.a: Hansa felt envious, wishing for the shiny cycle and the attention Leela got.

qa.q: What small steps does Hansa plan?
qa.a: Hansa plans to ask Papa to fix the bell and raise the seat, and to tell Leela sincerely that her cycle is nice.

qa.q: How might Leela have felt when Hansa said the cycle was too big?
qa.a: Leela might have felt hurt or confused by the unkind comment.

grounding: A child writes about envying a friend's new cycle and the attention it brings.

passage:
At the Gurpurab gathering in the village near Tarn Taran, Uma sang a shabad, and everyone praised her voice. Even the granthi ji nodded.

Gurpreet, eleven, sat at the back. He had practised the same shabad for weeks, but nobody asked him to sing.

"Uma sings like a bird," his Bibi said on the way home.

Gurpreet kicked a stone. "Why is she always the best at everything?"

Bibi looked at him. "Do you want her voice, or do you want to sing?"

He thought about it. "I want to sing."

"Then sing for me tonight."

qa.q: What did Uma sing?
qa.a: Uma sang a shabad.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet feel when everyone praised Uma?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt envious and left out, wishing he had her voice and praise.

qa.q: How did Bibi help Gurpreet with his envy?
qa.a: She asked whether he wanted Uma's voice or to sing himself, turning envy into his own goal.

qa.q: How might Uma feel if she knew about Gurpreet's feelings?
qa.a: Uma might feel surprised, as she was just singing and not trying to outdo anyone.

grounding: During Gurpurab, a boy envies a peer's praised singing, and his grandmother helps him turn it into his own goal.

passage:
The Christmas holidays in Lagos were hot, and every afternoon the boys played football on the street. This year, Jamal had new boots, bright orange with white stripes.

Everyone wanted to be on Jamal's team. They cheered his kicks.

Chidi, eleven, played in old canvas shoes with a hole at the toe. He scored two goals, but nobody noticed.

At home he said to his mother, "I want boots like Jamal's."

"Why?"

He thought. "So they'll cheer for me."

His mother smiled. "You scored two goals today. I heard from the window."

qa.q: What colour were Jamal's boots?
qa.a: Bright orange with white stripes.

qa.q: How did Chidi feel when everyone cheered for Jamal?

qa.q: How might Jamal see the attention he got?
qa.a: Jamal might enjoy it without noticing that Chidi felt left out.

grounding: During the Christmas holidays, a boy envies a friend's new boots and the attention they bring.

passage:
I remember the day I got my team jersey. I was eleven, and I'd been trying to get into the school football team for a whole year.

After practice, Aparna, the captain, threw a jersey at me. "Number 7. You're in."

I held it and couldn't speak. Then the others clapped, and someone put an arm round my shoulders.

That night I wore it to bed. For the first time at school, I didn't feel like the odd one out. I felt like part of something.

I'm Hafsa, and I still have that jersey in my cupboard.

qa.q: What number was on Hafsa's jersey?
qa.a: Number 7.

qa.q: How did Hafsa feel when the team clapped?
qa.a: Hafsa felt overwhelmed with joy and accepted, like part of something.

grounding: A child remembers the security and joy of being accepted into the school football team.

passage:
Swimming camp note, summer.

Farida joined the camp late, in the second week, and spent the first days sitting alone at the edge of the pool during breaks.

On Thursday, the group of girls she swims with invited her to their relay team. They practised the handover together and cheered when she finished her lap.

Since then, Farida walks in smiling and sits with them at break. Her mother told me she talks about the "relay girls" all evening.

I've kept the relay team together for the final. — Manjula

passage:
Ganesh Chaturthi, day 3

Today Kavitha Didi asked if I wanted to join the building dhol group! Only the big kids play in it, and I've been watching them from the balcony for two years.

She gave me the smallest dhol and showed me the beat. I got it wrong at first. Nobody laughed. They just played slower till I caught up.

When we played for the aarti, everyone in the building clapped. Kavitha Didi winked at me.

I didn't want to go home. I kept thinking, I'm one of them now.

Pooja

passage:
Teacher's note, Wednesday.

After the class reading test, Sarita put her head down on the desk. When I asked, she said, "Everyone reads faster than me. I'm the worst."

She had compared her score with three friends. She reads more slowly, but her understanding answers were among the best in class.

I showed her those answers and said reading fast and reading well aren't the same. She sat up a little.

I'll give her a reading buddy and check in weekly.

— Rekha

qa.q: What did Sarita say after the reading test?
qa.a: She said, "Everyone reads faster than me. I'm the worst."

qa.q: How did Sarita feel after comparing her score with her friends?
qa.a: Sarita felt inferior and discouraged, believing she was the worst.

qa.q: How did Rekha help Sarita?
qa.a: Rekha showed her strong answers and explained that reading well matters as much as reading fast.

qa.q: How might Sarita's friends see her reading?
qa.a: They might not realise she felt so bad, since they only compared speed.

grounding: A teacher notes a child feeling inferior after comparing her reading speed with peers, and offers perspective.

passage:
Winter sports day, Friday

Came last in the 100 metres. LAST. Kashish came first, again. Everyone crowded round her.

I stood by the water cooler and felt like the slowest person in the world. Why is she good at everything? Running, maths, drawing. I'm not good at anything.

Then Kashish came over. "You ran really straight. I always wobble." I don't know if she was just being nice.

Mumma says I'm good at looking after the class plants. That's not a sport. But still.

Alka

qa.a: Kashish came first.

qa.q: How did Alka feel after coming last?
qa.a: Alka felt inferior and defeated, like the slowest person in the world.

qa.a: Mumma could keep noticing Alka's real strengths and remind her that everyone is good at different things.

qa.q: How might Kashish feel coming over to Alka?
qa.a: Kashish may have felt kind and wanted to encourage Alka.

passage:
During the summer holidays, Avni came from Mumbai to the village near Sagar. She spoke English fast, wore shiny sandals, and knew the names of every cricket player.

Vijay, eleven, sat on the charpai in his old rubber slippers. When Avni asked him a question in English, he answered in Hindi and felt his face go hot.

That evening he told his Dadi, "She's better than me at everything."

Dadi said, "Can she milk a buffalo? Can she find the way to the river in the dark?"

Vijay laughed. "No."

"Then teach her tomorrow."

passage:
Friday

I'm SO angry. In the class quiz, Vikas looked at the answer sheet on Ma'am's desk when she left the room. I saw him. He got full marks and a star.

I got 8 out of 10 and I did it honestly.

I told Ma'am after class. She said she'd look into it. But I still feel hot inside. It's not fair. Rules are rules.

Didi says maybe Ma'am will handle it quietly. I hope so. I just want the star to go to someone who earned it.

Ganga

passage:
During Losar in the village near Dharamshala, the children played kabaddi in the monastery ground. Zeenat, eleven, was on the other team.

Tenzin crossed the line, got tagged, and then said, "I wasn't touched!"

Zeenat's face went red. "You were! Everyone saw!"

"No, I wasn't."

"That's cheating!" She stamped her foot. The game stopped.

An older monk walked over. "What happened?" Several children pointed at Tenzin. Tenzin looked down and walked off the field.

Zeenat was still breathing hard, but she said, "Okay, let's play again."

qa.a: They played kabaddi in the monastery ground.

passage:
In Istanbul during Ramadan, the queue at the bakery for fresh pide was long before iftar. Sami, ten, and his sister Elif had waited twenty minutes.

A man walked straight to the front and asked for three loaves.

Sami's fists clenched. "Hey! There's a line!"

Elif pulled his arm. "Sami, shh."

"But it's not fair! We waited!"

The baker looked at the man. "Please join the line, sir." The man frowned and went to the back.

Sami let out a breath. Elif whispered, "You were right. But you were loud."

qa.q: How long had Sami and Elif waited?

qa.q: How did Sami feel when the man cut in line?
qa.a: Sami felt angry and indignant at the unfairness, clenching his fists.

qa.a: He could speak firmly but quietly, or ask the baker for help, instead of shouting.

"What's this?"

"My science notes. You missed three days when you had fever. The test is on Monday."

Samir flipped through. Every page was neat, with diagrams. "You copied all this for me?"

"I made a second copy last night."

"That must have taken hours."

Zainab shrugged. "You'd do it for me."

passage:
The Diwali I was nine, I tore my new lehenga on the gate just before the puja. I cried so loudly that the neighbours came out.

Kavitha Aunty from next door took one look, went home, and came back with her sewing kit. She sat on our steps under the bulb and fixed it in ten minutes. You could hardly see the stitches.

I remember hugging her so hard she laughed. She didn't have to help. She had her own puja to do.

I'm Shreya, and every Diwali I take Kavitha Aunty the first box of sweets.

passage:

passage:
"Rashmi, you brought your phone?" Mehak whispered on the picnic bus.

"No. We all agreed, no phones this picnic."

"But Tanu brought hers."

"That's Tanu's choice. We voted."

On the way back, Ma'am said, "Thank you to everyone who kept our promise."

Rashmi sat up straighter. "See? It felt good to keep it."

passage:
The Holi I was ten, our colony had one rule: no colour on anyone who says no.

Gargi, from the corner house, said no. She was wearing her school uniform because she was going for tuition.

My friend Bunty picked up a handful of green anyway. I grabbed his wrist. "She said no. That's the rule."

He was annoyed. "It's Holi!"

"Rules are for Holi too."

He dropped it. Later, Gargi waved at me from her gate.

I'm Pankaj, and I remember walking home feeling taller.

qa.q: What was the colony's rule?
qa.a: No colour on anyone who says no.

qa.q: How did Pankaj feel walking home?
qa.a: Pankaj felt proud and good, like standing taller, for upholding the rule.

passage:
Dhruv, you lost your race today, na? Sit. Let your Swati Nani tell you something.

When I was eleven, the school winter sports day had a 400-metre race. I came last. Last! The whole school saw me.

I cried behind the shed. My father found me. He didn't say "don't cry". He said, "Do you want to run again next year?"

I did. So every morning that winter, before school, I ran round our field. Some mornings I hated it.

Next year, I came third. Not first. But I ran past the shed where I had cried.

So, Dhruv. Cry today. Tomorrow, run.

qa.q: Where did young Swati cry?
qa.a: She cried behind the shed.

qa.q: How did young Swati feel coming last?
qa.a: Young Swati felt ashamed and upset, crying behind the shed.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Swati's story?
qa.a: Her father asking whether she wanted to run again led her to practise every morning that winter.

qa.q: How might Swati's father have felt finding her crying?
qa.a: Her father likely felt caring and wanted to encourage her without dismissing her feelings.

passage:
The monsoon had turned the cricket ground to mud. Gautam's under-12 team lost the final by two runs, and he was the last batsman out.

He sat in the rain on the boundary, head in his hands. His coach, Ira Ma'am, sat beside him.

"I let everyone down."

"You made 18. The top score."

"But I got out."

"You'll get out a hundred times. What will you do tomorrow?"

Gautam thought. "Practice."

The next morning, the rain was still falling. Gautam was at the nets at seven.

qa.q: How did Gautam feel after being the last batsman out?

qa.q: How might Gautam's teammates see his score?
qa.a: His teammates might see his 18 as the best effort, not a failure.

grounding: In the monsoon, a boy bounces back from a cricket loss with steady effort.

passage:

passage:
Lohri party note.

At the class Lohri party, Baljeet tripped carrying peanuts and spilled them everywhere. Sabina said, "Wow, great job, Baljeet!" with a big smile.

A year ago, Baljeet might have cried. Today he looked at her, saw her grin, and said, "Thank you, I practise every day." Everyone laughed, including Sabina.

He understood it was teasing, not meanness. They picked up the peanuts together, still giggling, and Baljeet saved the last handful for Sabina. — class teacher

Eid, Monday

Arnab Bhai came for sheer khurma. The first thing he said was, "Parveen, you're so tall now, can you see Lahore from there?"

Last year I would have felt bad. I'm the tallest in my class and people tease me.

But today I saw he was smiling and his eyes were kind. So I said, "Yes, and I can see your bald spot too."

He laughed so much he spilled his sheer khurma. Ammi laughed too.

I think teasing is okay when you both laugh.

Parveen

Class teacher's note, Tuesday.

Our class library runs on trust: children borrow books and return them by Friday, and nobody checks.

Yusuf finished his book early but kept it to read again. On Friday, he brought it back even though he wanted it longer. When I asked, he said, "If I keep it, someone else can't read it. And then nobody will trust the library."

I told him he could borrow it again next week. — Kiran

qa.a: Yusuf felt a bit reluctant, wanting to read it again, but responsible to the class.

qa.a: They would feel trusted and fairly treated, knowing books come back on time.

Summer holidays, Thursday

Played the board game with Uday all afternoon. When I went to get water, he said, "Let's move my token three extra places, nobody will know."

I said no. He said I was boring.

But if we cheat, the game doesn't mean anything. And next time he'd cheat against me.

So we played properly. I lost. It was still fun.

At the end Uday said, "Okay, you're right. It's better when it's fair."

Sunaina

qa.a: Uday wanted to move his token three extra places.

qa.a: Sunaina felt a bit hurt but firm, believing cheating would spoil the game.

qa.q: What did Sunaina understand about rules?
qa.a: That rules only work when everyone trusts each other, and cheating would make the game meaningless.

qa.q: How did Uday's view change?
qa.a: Uday first wanted to cheat but later agreed it was better when it's fair.

grounding: A child refuses to cheat in a game because rules work only when players trust each other.

During the wheat harvest, the handpump in the village near Bareilly had a long line of children with buckets. Sunaina, ten, was fifth.

Farhan came late. "My Abbu needs water fast for the thresher. Let me go first."

Sunaina looked at the line. "Everyone's parents are in the fields."

"But I'm older."

"Then you know the rule. We go in turn."

The others nodded. Farhan huffed but joined the back.

When Sunaina's turn came, she filled her bucket quickly, then helped Farhan carry his to the front of the line when it was his turn.

qa.q: What position was Sunaina in line?
qa.a: Sunaina was fifth.

qa.q: How did Sunaina feel when Farhan asked to go first?
qa.a: Sunaina felt calm but determined, and a little annoyed, believing the rule should apply to everyone.

qa.q: What did Sunaina do that showed fairness and kindness?
qa.a: She kept the turn rule, then helped Farhan carry his bucket when it was his turn.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel after joining the back?
qa.a: Farhan might feel annoyed at first but later grateful for Sunaina's help.

grounding: During the harvest, a girl upholds a fair turn-taking rule at a village handpump based on mutual trust.
